Here is the full integrated 12-week plan summary, combining the vegan muscle-gain program, weekly structure, resistance training details, cardio, nutrition, cheat meals, post-workout options, and progression guidance. It’s designed for a 26-year-old vegan recreational lifter with full gym access, targeting approximately 150 g protein/day from plant sources, and with a plan that includes phased progression and a phase-3 intensity push.

Overall goals and structure
- Primary goal: Muscle gain (hypertrophy) with progressive overload while maintaining conditioning and recovery on a vegan diet.
- Training frequency: 4 days/week of resistance training (Upper A, Lower A, Upper B, Lower B) with optional 5th day for accessories/mobility.
- Phases:
  - Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4): Foundation, technique, moderate hypertrophy volume, establish routine, solid protein intake.
  - Phase 2 (Weeks 5–9): Progressive overload, higher volume/difficulty, structured progression, optional microupright tests to inform loads.
  - Phase 3 (Weeks 10–12): Peak hypertrophy with intensity push, advanced overload techniques (tempo, density, rest-pauses, cluster sets), tighter RIR targets, deliberate deload in Week 12.
- Cardio: 2–3 sessions/week, integrated with lifting days or rest days, including steady-state, tempo/intervals, and optional low-impact cardio to support recovery and conditioning.
- Nutrition: 
  - Daily protein target ~150 g (from plant sources).
  - Slight caloric surplus to support muscle gain; adjust for cardio demand and individual rate of gain.
  - Supplements as needed (vegan protein powder, B12, D3, omega-3 DHA/EPA algae, possibly iron after ferritin check, creatine monohydrate 5 g/day).
  - Cheat meal day structure: included in Phase 2/early Phase 3 optionally; see cheat meal section below.

Weekly training structure
- Day 1: Upper A
- Day 2: Lower A
- Day 3: Rest or Mobility/Light cardio
- Day 4: Upper B
- Day 5: Lower B
- Day 6–7: Rest or optional 5th day (Accessory/Mobility/Conditioning)

Phase 1: Foundation and Technique (Weeks 1–4)
Goals: Build technique, establish hypertrophy stimulus, start progressive overload, lock in 150 g/day protein.

Key weekly targets
- Reps: Most sets in the 6–12 range; primary lifts 6–8 reps for strength-endurance within hypertrophy.
- Rest: 60–90 seconds for most accessory work; 2–3 minutes for main compounds if needed.
- Core work: 2–3 sessions/week (anti-rotation and bracing).
- Core lifts (examples):
  - Upper A: Barbell bench press 4x6–8; seated overhead press 3x8–10; barbell row 3x8; lat pulldown 3x10; incline DB fly 3x10; curls 2x12; triceps pushdown 2x12.
  - Lower A: Back squat 4x6–8; Romanian deadlift 3x8; leg press or lunges 3x10; leg curl 3x12; calf raise 4x12.
  - Core: Plank variations, side planks.

Phase 2: Progressive Overload and Volume Build (Weeks 5–9)
Goals: Increase weekly volume and intensity; introduce occasional load tests; use tempo and density work to intensify stimulus.

Weekly structure with progression
- Week 5: Main lifts in 4x6–8; add 1–2 accessory movements; introduce light tempo on key lifts.
- Week 6: Reps in the 6–10 range where possible; add tempo (3–0–1–0) on major lifts; minor progression in load.
- Week 7: Increase weights 2.5–5% where able; maintain 6–8 reps on main lifts.
- Week 8: Back-off or back-off sets on top sets at 70–75% for 8–12 reps.
- Week 9: Optional 1–RM style test on a core lift to recalibrate loads; adjust Week 10 plan accordingly.

Phase 3: Peak Hypertrophy and Intensification (Weeks 10–12)
Goals: Maximize hypertrophy with higher intensity, closer-to-failure training, and density work; then taper.

Key changes for Phase 3
- Main lifts: Upper A 4x6–8; Lower A 4x6–8; Upper B 3–4x8–10; Lower B 3–4x8–10.
- Intensity techniques (rotate weekly): 
  - Post-activation potentiation (PAP) preload: 1 heavy rep at 90–95% of top weight, then drop to work weight.
  - Tempo variations: 3-0-2-0 or 4-0-1-0 on key lifts.
  - Rest-pause: after near-failure, rest 10–15 seconds to complete 2–3 more reps.
  - Density sets: 2 back-to-back sets with 15–30 seconds rest between.
  - Cluster sets: 4x4 with 15–20s intra-set rest.
- RIR targets:
  - Main lifts: aim for 1–2 RIR by Week 10; progress to 0–1 RIR by Week 11–12 where technique remains solid.
  - Accessory lifts: 1–2 RIR with occasional 0–1 on select sets if joints tolerate.
- Week-by-week highlights:
  - Week 10: Introduce at least one intensity technique per session on 1–2 lifts.
  - Week 11: Push closer to failure on major lifts; include density block on at least one exercise per session.
  - Week 12: Deload with reduced volume (40–50%); maintain light intensity techniques to preserve neural drive without fatigue.

Cardio in Phase 3
- Maintain 2–3 cardio sessions/week as per Phase 1/2.
- If resistance-work intensity is high, swap one high-intensity cardio session for restorative low-impact work (walks, easy cycling).

Nutrition in Phase 3
- Calories: Slight surplus maintained; when high-intensity days are heavy, consider a modest calorie bump (100–250 kcal).
- Protein: Maintain ~150 g/day; ensure 40–60 g protein per main meals and post-workout shakes around high-load days.
- Carbs: Increase around high-intensity days to support glycogen needs (4–6 g/kg/day depending on body weight and tolerance).
- Hydration: Maintain electrolyte balance on higher training loads.

Cheat meal day (structure option)
- Frequency: One cheat day day every 2–3 weeks; place on a low–to moderate-load training day or rest day.
- Target: 1,000–1,500 kcal above typical daily intake; hit ~150 g protein across the day; emphasize carbs and fats from vegan sources.
- Example: Week 6 cheat day; protein kept high, calories increased with enjoyable vegan meals; avoid extreme binge to prevent adverse fatigue or digestion issues. Alternatively, two lighter cheat meals (Weeks 4 and 9) with 500–800 kcal surplus each, if preferred.

Post-workout meals
- Aim for 25–40 g protein within 60–120 minutes after training, plus 40–60 g carbs to replenish glycogen.
- Options included: protein shakes with banana and fortified plant milk; rice bowls with tempeh/tofu; lentil/falafel plate with grains; smoothie bowls with protein; chickpea pancakes; etc.
- Vegan proteins: pea+rice blends or other complete-profile blends; consider 1–2 shakes on heavy days to hit daily 150 g target.

Sample days and progression reminders
- Example upper-lower split in Week 1:
  - Day 1 Upper A: Bench 4x6–8, Overhead press 3x8, Barbell row 3x8, Lat pulldown 3x10, Incline DB fly 3x10, curls 2x12, tricep pushdown 2x12.
  - Day 2 Lower A: Back squat 4x6–8, RDL 3x8, Leg press 3x10, Leg curl 3x12, Calf raises 4x12.
  - Day 4 Upper B: Incline bench 4x6–8, Lateral raises 3x12, Cable row 3x8–10, Face pulls 3x12, Chest-supported row 3x12, Dips/skull crushers 2x12.
  - Day 5 Lower B: Deadlift variation 3–4x5–6, Front goblet squat 3x8, Hip thrust 3x10, Leg extensions 3x12, Calf raises 4x12.
- Phase 3 Week 10 example: 0–1 RIR on main sets; add 1 intensity technique (PAP preload or tempo) on one exercise per session; include a density block on one lift.
- Phase 3 Week 12 deload: 40–50% volume reduction; light sets with moderate resistance; focus on mobility and technique.

Monitoring and auto-regulation
- Track weekly: weights lifted, reps achieved, perceived exertion, fatigue, sleep, appetite, GI comfort, and mood.
- If technique degrades or joints hurt, reduce volume or revert to simpler variations and postpone intensity techniques.
- Adjust calories if weight is rising too fast or not at all; keep protein fixed at ~150 g/day.

Optional customization notes
- If you share her current body weight, available equipment (e.g., cable machines, leg extension/curl, free weights), injury history, and preference for certain lifts, I can translate this into a precise week-by-week calendar with exact weight targets, progression notes, and a meal-by-meal vegan plan aligned to 150 g protein/day.
- If she wants a different cheat-day placement (Weeks 4 and 9 instead of Week 6), I can restructure Phase 2 accordingly.

Next steps and deliverables
- I can provide a precise week-by-week calendar with: per-session exercise lists, set/rep schemes, progression targets, and recommended weights based on estimated 1RM or surrogate reps in reserve.
- I can also generate a full 7–day rotating meal plan with exact gram-by-gram ingredients to consistently hit 150 g protein/day, plus a shopping list.

Great question. For a vegan client aiming for ~150 g protein/day, the right protein powder can be a big help with convenience and meeting targets. Here are practical guidelines and some product-type recommendations.

Key considerations
- Protein quality and completeness: Look for blends that provide a complete amino acid profile or pair a complementary blend (e.g., pea + rice) to approach complete protein.
- Protein content per scoop: Most vegan powders range 20–35 g protein per scoop. You’ll want 25–35 g per scoop to hit daily targets with relatively few shakes.
- Digestibility: Some people do better with pea, others with rice or a blend. If GI issues or gas occur, consider trying different bases (pea isolate, rice protein, or a blend) or using half-scoops.
- Flavor and mixability: Since you’ll use this daily, pick a flavor you enjoy and a formula that mixes well with water or plant milk.
- Additives: Check for added sugars, artificial sweeteners, and unnecessary fillers. Look for powders with clean ingredient lists.
- Fortifications: Some vegan proteins include added B12, iron, calcium, and sometimes digestive enzymes; not essential but a bonus.
- Allergies and preferences: Ensure no gluten if sensitive; some blends include gluten-containing ingredients.

Common vegan protein bases
- Pea protein: High in leucine, good amino profile, typically easy to digest.
- Rice protein: Generally gentle on the stomach, but lower in lysine; blends often pair well with pea.
- Soy protein: Complete amino acid profile and high leucine, but some avoid due to thyroid or allergen concerns.
- Hemp protein: Good omega-3 content and fiber, but typically lower protein per scoop.
- Blends: Pea + rice or pea + rice + hemp to balance amino acids, improve texture, and often taste.

Recommended product types (scenarios)
- Best overall flexibility: Pea + rice blend (often 25–28 g protein per scoop; smooth texture, good mixability in water or plant milk).
- Best for taste and texture: Blended plant proteins marketed as "protein blend" with vanilla/cocoa flavors; many include 20–25 g per scoop but are delicious and easy to drink post-workout.
- If you want extra inclusions: A blend that includes added BCAA or EAA profile, plus vitamins/minerals (watch for added sugars).
- If you’re sensitive to texture: Isolate formulations tend to mix smoother than concentrates; choose a pea or pea+rice isolate.

Practical recommendations to try (brands commonly well-regarded in vegan space)
- Profesional/athlete-grade blends:
  -vegan peptide/protein blends (pea + rice): widely available from brands like Vega Sport, Nuzest Clean Lean Protein (pea + rice), KOS, Vega One
- Pea protein isolates:
  - Transparent Labs Plant Protein, Myvegan, INISFA
- Pea + rice blends:
  - Nuzest Clean Lean Protein (pearl barley-free), Orgain Organic Protein & Superfood (pea + brown rice blend)
- Mixed blends with added nutrients:
  - Vega Sport Premium Protein, Garden of Life Organic Protein (raw, plant-based blends)
- Budget-friendly:
  - Myprotein Plant Protein Isolate, NOW Sports Pea Protein Isolate
Note: Availability varies by country. Check for certified vegan labeling and third-party testing if possible.

How to choose for her plan
- Start with a pea + rice blend or a dedicated vegan protein blend with at least 25 g protein per scoop and 3–5 g of BCAAs per serving.
- Choose a flavor you’ll enjoy post-workout and in smoothies; consider pairing with fortified plant milk to help hit calcium and vitamin D needs.
- If she trails on daily protein, you can use a 2nd shake on heavier lift days to ensure 150 g total, especially around workouts.

Practical dosing tips
- Use 1–2 scoops per day depending on protein powder protein-per-scoop and meal planning. If a powder provides 25 g per scoop, you can plan one post-workout and one to two other meals as needed to reach 150 g/day.
- If she uses creatine (recommended, vegan, 5 g/day), time it consistently regardless of protein shake timing.

Safety and substitutions
- If she has gut sensitivity, start with 1/2 scoops for a week, then gradually increase.
- Keep an eye on total calories; some protein powders add extra calories; adjust meals accordingly if weight gain is not desired.

Next steps

Sure—adding a structured cheat meal day can help with adherence, social flexibility, and occasional a metabolic reset, while still keeping the 12-week plan on track for muscle gain on a vegan diet.

Notes and philosophy
- Purpose: Provide a periodic, planned high-calorie, enjoyable meal to satisfy cravings, support adherence, and occasionally restore glycogen/calories without derailing progress.
- Frequency: One “cheat meal day” every 2–3 weeks works well for many clients without compromising hypertrophy progress. For a 12-week plan, I’ll propose 1 full cheat meal day (e.g., Week 6) or 2 lighter cheat meals spread across Weeks 4 and 9, depending on preference.
- Calorie impact: A single cheat meal typically adds 700–1200+ calories, depending on choices. If you anticipate larger cravings on weekends or social events, you can shift the plan to align with those days.

Cheat meal day structure (Option A: single cheat day, Week 6)
- Timing: Choose a day with lower planned training load (e.g., a rest day or a lighter lower-body day) or the day after a lower-intensity session to minimize fatigue.
- Calorie target: 1,000–1,500 kcal above the usual daily maintenance on that day, while keeping protein intake high (still hit ~150 g protein across the day). The added calories should come mostly from carbohydrates and some fats.
- Protein: Maintain protein goal for the day (~150 g) to preserve muscle protein synthesis. Spread protein across meals as usual.
- Carbohydrate strategy: Emphasize carbohydrate-rich vegan foods to support glycogen replenishment and provide satiety for the cheat meal.
- Fat: Include a reasonable amount of fats (8–25 g) within the extra calories to avoid too extreme a surge.
- Example cheat-day plan (illustrative):
  - Breakfast: Protein-rich smoothie bowl with extra fruit and granola; add a dessert option later in the day if desired.
  - Lunch: Large lentil/chickpea grain bowl with quinoa, sweet potato, veggies, tahini sauce.
  - Snack: Bagel with vegan cream cheese and smoked paprika, or a substantial vegan burrito with rice, beans, avocado.
  - Dinner: Tempeh/tofu dish with rice or pasta, a rich sauce (tomato-olive-oil) and garlic bread.
  - Dessert/appetizer: A piece of vegan cheesecake or ice cream; small to medium portion.
  - Ensure hydration and include fiber sources to mitigate GI stress.

Cheat meal day structure (Option B: two lighter cheat meals, Week 4 and Week 9)
- On each cheat day, allow two indulgent meals, spaced out by 4–6 hours, with protein targets still met and overall daily calories increased by about 500–800 kcal.
- This approach can be gentler on digestion and easier to plan around social events.

Implementation tips
- Plan in advance: Have a list of vegan-friendly indulgences you’ll allow on cheat days (e.g., vegan pizza with extra toppings, plant-based burgers with fries, cinnamon buns, cookies, or vegan ice cream).
- Protein continuity: Even during cheat meals, include some protein to maintain the daily target (e.g., a protein shake or a higher-protein entrée within the day).
- Training around cheat day: If the cheat day falls near a workout, you can time the larger carb intake to post-workout to aid glycogen replenishment and recovery.
- Track impact: Monitor weight, mood, digestion, sleep, and training performance in the days following a cheat meal day. If there’s a noticeable rebound in weight or fatigue, adjust frequency or portion sizes accordingly.

Training and nutrition adjustments
- If weight gain accelerates too quickly after cheat days, reduce future cheat-day calories by 100–200 kcal or move cheat days further apart.
- If appetite or energy remains consistently high during diet days, you can maintain the same structure and simply allow more flexible options on cheat days.
- Ensure fiber intake remains stable (to reduce GI distress) by including vegetables and fruits on cheat days.

Safety and considerations
- If the client has a history of disordered eating or is prone to binge patterns, approach cheat meals with caution and keep them as planned, controlled indulgences rather than unstructured eating.
- Hydration remains important; maintain water intake and consider electrolytes if cheat meals increase salt intake significantly.

Got it. Pushing intensity in Phase 3 (Weeks 10–12) can help maximize hypertrophy while still protecting recovery. Here’s an updated approach that preserves the 12-week structure but raises stimulus in Phase 3 through advanced overload methods, tighter RIR targets, and occasional density work.

What changes to Phase 3 (Weeks 10–12)
- Overall goal: maintain or increase training intensity, improve time under tension, and capitalize on accumulated base by adding higher-effort sets and short rest blocks.
- Main lifts: keep 4x6–8 for Upper A and Lower A, and 3–4x8–10 for Upper B and Lower B, but incorporate intensity techniques and density work within these sets.
- Intensity techniques: choose 1–2 per week per mesocycle (weeks 10–12) and rotate to avoid overuse.
  - Post-activation potentiation (PAP) style preload: 1 set of heavier load at 90–95% of top weight for 1–2 reps, then drop to working weight for 4–6 reps.
  - Tempo variations: 3-0-2-0 ecc or 4-0-1-0 to increase time under tension.
  - Rest-pauses: after reaching near-failure on final rep, rest 10–15 seconds and complete 2–3 more reps.
  - Density sets: perform 2 back-to-back sets with 15–30 seconds rest between, e.g., top set to near-failure, then a back-off set with the same weight.
  - Cluster sets: 4x4 with short intra-set rests (15–20 seconds) to accumulate more total reps at near-max loads.
- RIR targets: shift to stricter proximity to failure.
  - Main lifts: aim for 1–2 RIR on work sets by Week 10, and 0–1 RIR by Week 11–12 on some sets (where technique remains solid).
  - Accessory lifts: 1–2 RIR, but you can push to 0–1 on select days if joints feel good.
- Volume and weekly structure:
  - Week 10: maintain 4x6–8 and 3–4x8–10, but add 1 intensity technique on 1–2 lifts per session.
  - Week 11: push closer to failure on major lifts with 1–2 intensity techniques; incorporate 1 density/cluster set on one exercise per session.
  - Week 12 (Deload option): still include intensity techniques but scale down overall volume by 40–50% and drop weight for a technique-only session to consolidate gains without excessive fatigue. If fatigue is high, consider moving deload to Week 11 or extending into Week 12.

Proposed Phase 3 (Weeks 10–12) week-by-week adjustments
- Week 10:
  - Upper A: 4x6–8
    - Example: Barbell bench 4x6–8, add 1 heavy rep with 90% of top weight for 1–2 reps (PAP) on first set, then 3–4 more sets at working load with 1–2 RIR.
  - Lower A: 4x6–8
    - Add tempo 3-0-1-0 on squats or deadlifts for 6–8 reps; then perform 1 density set on a single leg or glute-focused accessory.
  - Upper B: 3–4x8–10
    - Introduce cluster sets on one exercise (e.g., dumbbell incline press: 4x6 with 20–30s rest between clusters).
  - Lower B: 3–4x8–10
    - Use rest-pauses on hip hinge accessory (e.g., Romanian deadlift 3x8 with 15s rest pauses after final reps).
- Week 11:
  - Bring intensity closer to failure:
    - Upper A: 4x6–8 with 0–1 RIR on top sets; add a PAP preload earlier in the week.
    - Lower A: 4x6–8 with 0–1 RIR on main sets; include a 1–2 set density block on a hip-dominant movement.
    - Upper B: 4x8–10 with 0–1 RIR on final rep; add a tempo or cluster set on one lift.
    - Lower B: 4x6–8 with 0–1 RIR; add an optional short interval finisher at the end of a leg day if energy allows.
- Week 12 (Deload with technique focus):
  - Reduce volume by 40–50% but keep a few intensity techniques at light loads to maintain neural drive without fatigue.
  - Example: 2–3 core lifts with 2–3 sets using 70–75% of 1RM, each with 1–2 reps at near-failure using cluster or tempo but lighter loads.

Cardio during Phase 3
- Maintain 2–3 cardio sessions/week as previously outlined, but be mindful of recovery.
- If intensity increases on resistance days, consider swapping one high-intensity cardio session for a restorative, low-impact session (walks, light cycling, or swimming) to preserve energy.

Nutrition during Phase 3
- Total calories: maintain a slight surplus or around maintenance with progressive overload; when intensity surges, consider a modest uptick (100–250 kcal/day) to support recovery.
- Protein: keep ~150 g/day; with higher intensity days, ensure 40–60 g protein per main meals and post-workout shakes to support MPS.
- Carbs: increase around higher-intensity days to replenish glycogen (target 4–6 g/kg/day depending on body weight and tolerance).
- Hydration and electrolytes: pay extra attention to hydration given higher training stress.
